enonce_markdown: A trader at the Bamenda market uses a strong magnet to pick out loose pieces of metal from a heap of rubbish. Which of these pieces will the magnet attract?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Only a few metals are magnetic: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Metals such as copper, aluminium, brass and zinc are not attracted by a magnet.

### Solution

Steel is made mostly of iron, so a steel nail is attracted. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, and aluminium and copper are non-magnetic metals, so none of them is attracted, however strong the magnet.

**Answer: a.**

choix.texte: A steel nail
A brass key
An aluminium drink can
A piece of copper wire

enonce_markdown: The north pole of a bar magnet P is brought near one end of a bar Q that hangs freely on a thread. The end of Q is pushed away from P. What can be concluded about Q?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Attraction happens between a magnet and any unmagnetised magnetic material, but **repulsion** only happens between two like poles. Repulsion is therefore the sure test that a bar is a magnet.

### Solution

The end of Q is repelled by a north pole, and only a north pole repels a north pole. So Q is itself a magnet and the end near P is a **north pole**.

- An unmagnetised iron bar would be attracted, never repelled.
- If the end were a south pole it would be attracted by the north pole of P.
- A bar of brass or copper would show no force at all.

**Answer: b.**

choix.texte: Q is an unmagnetised iron bar.
Q is a magnet and the end near P is a north pole.
Q is a magnet and the end near P is a south pole.
Q is made of a non-magnetic material such as brass.

enonce_markdown: The electromagnet of a crane at a scrap yard in Douala must lift steel scrap when the current is switched on and drop it when the current is switched off. Which material should be used for the core of this electromagnet?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

An electromagnet needs a core that is magnetised strongly when the current flows and loses its magnetism when the current stops. This is a **soft** magnetic material. A **hard** magnetic material such as steel keeps its magnetism and is used for permanent magnets.

### Solution

Soft iron is magnetised easily by the current and loses almost all its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the scrap is dropped.

- Copper is a very good conductor but it is not magnetic, so it gives no strong electromagnet.
- Steel would be magnetised by the current but would stay magnetised afterwards, and the scrap would not drop.
- Aluminium is light but it is not a magnetic material.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: Copper, because it is a very good conductor of electricity.
Steel, because it keeps its magnetism after the current is switched off.
Aluminium, because it is light.
Soft iron, because it is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

enonce_markdown: A strong bar magnet lies on a table. A small plotting compass is placed on the line through the axis of the magnet, close to its north pole and beyond the end of the magnet. The magnet is so strong that the magnetic field of the Earth can be ignored. In which direction does the north-seeking end of the compass needle point?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Magnetic field lines leave the north pole of a magnet and enter its south pole. A compass needle lines up with the field line through its position, and its north-seeking end points in the direction of the field.

### Solution

At a point on the axis, just beyond the north pole, the field line through the compass runs straight out of the north pole, away from the magnet. The north-seeking end of the needle points along this direction, so it points **directly away from the magnet along its axis**.

This also agrees with the rule that like poles repel: the north end of the needle is pushed away by the north pole of the magnet and its south end is pulled towards it.

- Pointing towards the north pole of the magnet would mean a north pole is attracted by a north pole, which is wrong.
- A direction at right angles to the axis is the direction at the middle of the magnet, not at its end.
- Pointing to the geographic north is the effect of the Earth's field, which is ignored here.

**Answer: a.**

choix.texte: Directly away from the magnet, along its axis.
Directly towards the north pole of the magnet.
At right angles to the axis of the magnet.
Towards the geographic north of the Earth.

enonce_markdown:
A technician wants to protect a sensitive measuring instrument from the magnetic field of a strong magnet near it. He decides to place the instrument inside a closed box.

(i) Name a material that is suitable for the box and one that is not. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Explain, using magnetic field lines, how the suitable box protects the instrument. *[3 marks]*

(iii) Explain why steel would be a poor choice for the box, even though it is a magnetic material. *[1 mark]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Magnetic field lines take the easiest path, and they pass much more easily through a magnetic material than through air. A thick shell of soft magnetic material therefore gathers the lines into its walls and leaves the space inside almost free of field: this is magnetic screening.

### Solution

(i) **Suitable:** soft iron. **Not suitable:** copper (or aluminium, brass, plastic): these are non-magnetic, so the field passes through them as if they were air.

(ii) The field lines of the strong magnet enter the iron walls of the box because iron lets them through much more easily than air. They are carried round inside the walls and leave on the other side, so very few lines cross the space inside the box. The magnetic field inside is almost zero and the instrument is not affected.

(iii) Steel is a hard magnetic material: it would stay magnetised after the strong magnet is removed, and the box would then become a permanent magnet with a field of its own. Soft iron loses its magnetism when the strong magnet is taken away.

enonce_markdown: A strong magnet is held with its north pole at the bottom. A soft-iron nail A hangs from this north pole. A second soft-iron nail B hangs from the lower end of nail A. Neither nail is magnetised to begin with. Which row gives the pole induced at the end of A that touches the magnet and the pole induced at the free lower end of B?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A magnetic material placed in a magnetic field is magnetised by induction: the end nearer to a pole of the magnet becomes the **opposite** pole, and the far end becomes the same pole as the magnet. The induced magnet then induces the next one in the same way.

### Solution

- Nail A touches a north pole, so the end touching the magnet becomes a **south** pole and the lower end of A becomes a **north** pole.
- Nail B hangs from the north pole at the lower end of A, so the upper end of B (touching A) becomes a **south** pole and the free lower end of B becomes a **north** pole.

The unlike poles at each joint attract each other, which is why the nails hang in a chain. If the magnet is removed, the soft-iron nails lose almost all their magnetism and fall apart.

The end of A touching the magnet is therefore a south pole, which rules out the rows that start with "north". The free end of B is a north pole, which rules out the row that ends with "south".

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: End of A touching the magnet: north. Free end of B: south.
End of A touching the magnet: north. Free end of B: north.
End of A touching the magnet: south. Free end of B: south.
End of A touching the magnet: south. Free end of B: north.
